All-atom molecular dynamics · superfolder GFP · 2026-08-24 00:56 UTC

A DNA spring, wound around a fluorescent protein

Two amber codons put a tetrazine amino acid6,7 on adjacent strands of sfGFP’s β-barrel1. A doubly-modified DNA duplex clicks onto both, and because dsDNA is far too stiff to follow the barrel’s curvature it has to bend — which should push the two attachment points apart. This is what that looks like atom by atom, across eleven DNA-bearing constructs in two proteins. The duplex turns out to deliver far more force than the model predicts, and the protein turns out not to care: every construct pulls its attachment sites slightly together, and it makes no measurable difference whether the DNA is a spring at all.

The construct

Asp133 · Asn149 · CRO 66 · 31.3 Å apart

The attachment sites are Asp133 and Asn149 in 2B3P’s numbering — D134 and N150 in the construct’s own, which runs one higher. They sit on adjacent strands of the barrel with His148 between them, and His148 donates a hydrogen bond straight to the chromophore’s phenolate oxygen2. That is the mechanical path from the DNA to the fluorescence, and it is why these two sites are the interesting ones rather than merely convenient ones.

A correction worth carrying back to the bench

The PyMOL session’s 134TAG and 150TAG selections point at Gly134 and Val150 — one residue off. The mass spectrometry29,6 settles it: the single construct is +141 Da (Asn → Tet2-Et) and the double +281 Da (= 141 + 140, Asn plus Asp). Gly → Tet2-Et would be +198 Da and Val → Tet2-Et +156 Da, and neither is observed. build/01_protein/fix_pse_selections.pml loads corrected selections over the session.

Every force here is Zocchi’s f(x)8,9,10 evaluated at the end-to-end distance the simulation itself settles at, not at an assumed one. The construct is not free to choose that distance arbitrarily — it is set by where the two tethers can reach — so this is the one number in the whole model that the simulation can supply independently.

The nick softens the spring in the model — but not in measurement

The nicked 40 bp duplex delivers 2.37 pN against 3.04 pN for the intact duplex of the same length, and it is visibly floppier: its span wanders over 4.1 Å within a trajectory against 3.7 Å for the intact one. Zocchi’s two values of the critical bending torque10,9 — 27 pN·nm with a nick, 31–36 without — predict this ordering, and we reach it here from structure rather than from his calibration.

Measured directly, though, the nick does nothing resolvable — see the next section. The agreement here is between two calculations that both take the nick's effect from the same critical torque, so it is a consistency check on our geometry rather than independent support for the model. The nicked spring is the low-stress reference his argument relies on, and our force field does not reproduce that it is softer.

Shorter spring, more force; longer spring, more stored energy

The 27 bp spring delivers 6.33 pN and stores 5.3 kBT; the 40 bp spring delivers less force (3.04 pN) but stores more energy (8.4 kBT). That is not a contradiction: force is the derivative of the energy with respect to the end-to-end distance, and the longer rod is bent through 127° against 45° — much more total curvature, spread over many more base pairs, so a larger integral with a shallower slope. All three energies, 5.1–10.0 kBT, bracket the 6.6 kBT Zocchi measured for the guanylate-kinase chimera11 by an entirely different route.

The duplex bends smoothly — it does not kink

Zocchi’s model8 places all three springs on its kinked branch, and the forces above come from that branch. The structures do not corroborate it on this timescale. Bending is spread evenly at 3–8° per step with no localised spike (figure 4), and of 27–40 base pairs only 0.03–0.83 are open at any instant — the duplex is intact. Three explanations are possible: the force field resists kinking, the timescale is too short, or the model puts the kinking threshold in the wrong place. The literature answers fairly clearly, and it is mostly the last two.

The curvature we impose is below where all-atom MD nucleates kinks

The duplexes are built at R = 41–44 Å and relax over the run to 37–41 Å, i.e. 4.8–5.2° per base-pair step (measured, one-turn smoothed, 18 replicates), equivalent to a 70–78 bp minicircle. That is essentially nucleosomal curvature — 42 Å and 4.6°/bp — and about 56% of the curvature at which all-atom MD nucleates kinks.

Correcting a correction

An earlier version of this page said 31–34 Å and 5.7–6.3°/bp, and a version after that "corrected" it to being 25% tighter than nucleosomal. Both were wrong: 31–34 Å was a figure I had carried over without checking it against the trajectories, and the numbers above are what the bend analysis actually reports. The conclusion is unaffected in direction and slightly strengthened in degree — we are further below the kinking threshold than either earlier version implied.

Converting each published criterion to a threshold radius through R = B/τc:

Zocchi’s τc is the most kink-friendly estimate in the field: it places the softening transition at a gentler bend than a nucleosome, where every independent estimate is 1.3–2.7× stiffer. The one directly comparable calculation — Curuksu et al.’s umbrella sampling on a bent linear duplex in the same force-field family — finds type II kinks only above 8.6–9.3° per step, which is almost twice the curvature we impose. On that criterion, not seeing a kink is the expected result rather than an anomaly.

45 ns is short by two to five orders of magnitude

Base-pair lifetimes measured by NMR imino exchange are 1–40 ms, so the per-pair opening rate is ~10²–10³ s⁻¹. For ~30 pairs in parallel across our 270 ns of aggregate sampling the expected number of opening events is 8×10⁻⁴ to 8×10⁻³. Seeing none is what unstressed kinetics predicts before bending is considered at all. Turning that around converts a null result into a bound: these data are consistent with a stress-induced reduction of the opening barrier of up to about 5 kBT, and cannot support more. Independently, published kink free energies of 12–22 kBT imply waiting times of microseconds to hundreds of milliseconds.

Published calibration points agree: kinks appear at 80–800 ns in nucleosomal loops held far more tightly than ours, and at 20–25 ns in 65 bp closed minicircles — but a 90 bp minicircle run for 11 µs at R ≈ 49 Å showed no kinks and no base-pair-level distortion at all.

We measured the threshold rather than arguing about it

Everything above is other people's numbers. The compression windows let us put ours beside them: hold the bare 27 bp duplex at a series of separations, from its contour length down to 64% compression, and ask at what curvature this force field starts breaking base pairs. The criterion was fixed before the runs — an internal pair, not the terminal two which fray in anything, open in more than 10% of frames.

The gentlest curvature at which any interior pair opens is 5.5°/bp. and every run opens above 8.7°/bp. 50 of 84 runs are excluded because the duplex sat within 85 % of the box's perpendicular width, where it can reach its own image.

Three things follow. The force field can kink — reproducibly, with the opened pair sitting at the maximum of the bend profile — so the possibility that AMBER with OL15 simply cannot support a kink is excluded by our own data rather than by argument.

There is no threshold; there is a probability. An earlier version of this page said the threshold was 6.7–8.3°/bp. That rested partly on the 27-mer's widest windows — 66 Å and beyond — which are exactly the rows showing no opening at low curvature, and every one of them sits outside what its solvent box can hold. With only valid windows, opening appears as low as 5.5°/bp and becomes certain — every run in the window — only above 8.7°/bp. The per-run observation is bimodal: a run either keeps every interior pair shut for its whole trajectory or opens one and holds it open 30–100 % of frames. So what varies smoothly with curvature is the probability of opening rather than its extent, which is what figure 5 plots — binned by each run's own curvature, where the table above groups by window. Curuksu et al.'s 8.6–9.3°/bp from biased sampling is where our probability has already reached 0.8, so the two agree about where kinking becomes the expected behaviour while ours shows a stochastic tail below it. Both are a long way from Zocchi's τc, which implies 2.6–3.0 — even our tail does not reach that.

And our chimera sits at 4.8–5.2°/bp, below the lowest curvature at which we ever see a pair open — which is the answer. The construct is not bent far enough, on this force field's own showing.

One detail that makes this a check rather than a coincidence: in the 27 bp duplex the kink lands on base pair 17 in 11 of its 14 openings, across independent windows and replicates. Base 17 is an adenine and the step into it is CpA — one of the three pyrimidine–purine steps (CpG, TpA, CpA) that Curuksu names as where roll preferentially localises. The other pair that opened, bp13, sits at a TpG step, also pyrimidine–purine. The force field is not breaking a pair at random under load; it picks exactly the dinucleotide steps the literature says it should.

The force field, honestly

There is a documented bias, and OL15 is specifically implicated: backbone-dihedral refinements favour B-form geometry even in non-helical contexts, and all AMBER variants overestimate persistence length with OL15 the stiffest of them. Twist-bend kinks also require local undertwisting, and the OL family was tuned to increase twist. So OL15 is plausibly the least kink-prone reasonable choice, and that deserves saying. But the magnitude is not enough to rescue the model: parmbsc0 and parmbsc1 are softer and also fail to kink at comparable curvature on 20–240× longer runs; parmbsc1’s free-energy landscape is sub-harmonic, i.e. more deformable than elasticity predicts; and CHARMM36, the alternative, has the opposite pathology of spurious base-pair disruption. No head-to-head comparison of kinking propensity across these force fields in a sharply bent duplex has been published — that is a real gap.

So the forces above remain model-dependent numbers. They are consistent with the model’s inputs; they do not confirm its mechanism. That is why the force is now also measured directly, below.

What the spring delivers, measured

the force field's own answer, not the model's

Every force above is Zocchi's f(x) evaluated at a simulated distance. That is a model, and the obvious question — put to us directly in review — is what the force field says if you simply ask it. So we did: a bare duplex, no protein, held at a series of separations by a harmonic restraint between the two linker nitrogens. The mean restraint force ⟨k(r − x₀)⟩ is the force the duplex exerts, with no model in between.

The force does not depend on how far you compress it

For all three duplexes, regressing force on separation gives no resolvable slope (p = 0.49, 0.29, 0.54). A constant load independent of compression is the signature of a buckled rod: once past its critical load an elastic rod does not stiffen, it just keeps folding at roughly the same force.

And the load it holds is the Euler load

The 27 bp duplex plateaus at 25.7 ± 1.0 pN against a classical Euler buckling load of 26.8 pN — a ratio of 0.96, with nothing fitted. The 40 bp pair land at 1.27 and 1.17 of theirs. Textbook elasticity, from an all-atom force field, with a persistence length nobody supplied.

This disagrees with the model the project is built on

Zocchi's kinked branch predicts 2.4–6.6 pN for these same duplexes at these same separations. We measure 26 pN for the 27 bp — roughly six times higher — and on the unyielded branch, which is the branch his model says the duplex has already left. On this timescale the duplex is not a softened, kinked spring; it is an elastic rod holding its buckling load.

Two consequences. The forces in the table above are, if anything, underestimates. And the reason the protein does not respond is not that the force is small — it is that even 26 pN moved these attachment sites less than the noise, because the barrel is stiff along that coordinate and the load is not applied along it.

Two restraint stiffnesses, one answer

Each separation was run at two restraint stiffnesses, 33 and 200 kJ mol⁻¹ nm⁻². The soft one is not really a constraint — the duplex settles 2–7 Å past its target — so if the measured force were an artefact of how hard we pulled, the two would sit on different curves. Plotted against the separation the duplex actually adopted, they agree (p = 0.37, 0.40, 0.90). That is the control that makes this a measurement of the duplex rather than of the restraint.

What the nick does — and does not do

Zocchi's model treats the nick as the key softening control, and predicts about 1.3× less force. Measured, there is no resolvable difference: 15.2 pN intact against 14.0 pN nicked, p = 0.66. A nick removes one backbone bond from a rod held together by 40 base pairs' worth of stacking; over 20–30 ns it does not measurably change the buckling load. The model's ordering may still be right on longer timescales, where a nick can act as a hinge — but our own data does not support quoting it as a validated control, and the model section above should be read with that in mind.

What this cannot say

These are 20–30 ns windows on bare duplexes. A kink that takes microseconds to nucleate would lower the plateau and is invisible here, so the Euler agreement is evidence about this timescale, not about equilibrium.

And the chimera's own separation — about 70 Å for the 27 bp — is outside the range we can sample validly, because a box big enough to hold a 27-mer at 70 Å without it touching its own periodic image is larger than the one these runs used. An earlier draft quoted a measured force at the chimera's geometry; that figure came from a window whose target was 87 % of the box width and it is withdrawn. Repeating those windows in a larger box is queued and waiting on GPU allocation.

The protein is stiff; how stiff, we can only bound

The axial clamp — a genuine constant force, E = −f·r, applied between the two Cβ atoms — gives a compliance of 0.0105 ± 0.0057 Å pN⁻¹ over 0–20 pN across 18 replicates. Its 95% confidence interval, [-0.0011, 0.0221], includes zero: at 45 ns per replicate the response is not resolved from noise, and the 4 pN point sitting below the 0 pN point in figure 1 is that noise made visible. What the data do support is a lower bound, κ > 107 kBT nm⁻², which lands on the ~100 kBT nm⁻² Zocchi’s activity measurements imply8. Under a few pN a protein this stiff should move by hundredths of an ångström, which is precisely why it cannot be measured this way in 45 ns — the honest conclusion is agreement with his stiffness and no more.

The spring does not move the sites more than an axial pull

Retraction

An earlier version of this page said the three chimeras sat +0.19, +0.52 and +0.59 Å from the zero-force clamp, monotonic in force at 0.13 Å pN⁻¹, and attributed the excess over a pure axial pull to a couple and a shear delivered through the two flexible tethers. That claim is withdrawn. It used the unclicked protein as its zero. Every chimera is clicked, and clicking alone moves the sites +0.65 Å — fifteen to thirty times any force effect. The physical argument was also unsound: at equilibrium a couple does no net work, and along Cβ–Cβ only the component of force along that coordinate can displace the mean. Thanks to Doeke Hekstra for catching both.

The right zero is the clicked, unloaded protein: same tether chemistry, same two modified residues, no DNA. Against it, every chimera sits at or below the control — the springs compress the attachment sites or leave them alone. Nothing survives a Bonferroni correction for the three comparisons.

The two baselines, for comparison: the clicked control sits at 32.274 ± 0.092 Å and the unclicked protein the old claim used at 31.607 ± 0.066 Å.

What the axial clamp measures instead: the barrel's stiffness

Clamping the same two Cβ at 0, 2.35 and 4.88 pN on the clicked topology gives a straight line at 6.9 mÅ pN⁻¹ (r² = 0.998), i.e. κ ≈ 350 kBT nm⁻². The longer six-point ladder on the unclicked protein is noisier (r² = 0.18) and gives ≈ 230 kBT nm⁻². Both say the barrel along this coordinate is two to three and a half times stiffer than the ~100 kBT nm⁻² Zocchi uses as a generic protein spring constant8. At 350 kBT nm⁻² a 4 pN spring moves the sites 0.03 Å — which is the whole reason this cannot be measured by watching an equilibrium distance in 50 ns.

The spring is not acting at a distance — it is touching the protein

If the chimeras differ from a matched axial pull, the difference cannot be a couple, for the reason above. The obvious alternative is that the duplex is a large charged object tethered two nanometres from the barrel and leaning on it. That is what it does:

The duplex is in contact with the protein in essentially every frame of every replicate, so whatever it does, it does not do at a distance. And the most compressed system is the nicked one, which delivers the least modelled force — a floppier duplex lies against the barrel more readily, which is the ordering a contact mechanism predicts and the reverse of a force mechanism.

But contact does not survive its own test

That ordering is one comparison, and an earlier version of this page used it to argue for contact as the mechanism. With eleven constructs measured against their own controls, the compression correlates with contact area no better than it does with force — r = +0.32, p = 0.33 — and constructs with no spring at all compress as much as those with one. The section Is it acting as a spring at all? below does that test properly; this paragraph is what the contact measurement shows, not what it explains.

The companion ubiquitin study reaches the same negative conclusion from the other direction13: a control bearing two separate short strands reproduced most of the circular chimera's NMR spectrum, pointing at local protein–DNA interaction rather than spring action. Agreeing that it is not spring action is firmer than either study's guess at what it is instead.

The single-stranded control, and a sign flip

an entropic spring pulls where a duplex pushes

Replacing the duplex with a single strand of the same span changes the sign of the mechanics, which makes it the sharpest available control. A bent duplex is an enthalpic spring: it is stiffer than the geometry it is forced into, so it pushes its anchors apart. A single strand is an entropic spring with a 1.5 nm persistence length: it has far more contour than it needs, so it coils, and it can only ever pull — and then only once stretched past its natural size.

strandntcontour (Å) natural rms end-to-end (Å)span held at (Å) tension (pN)state
50 nt ssDNA, closed loop502959454.30 — slackslack
50 nt ssDNA, closed loop502959441.70 — slackslack

Both single-stranded loops sit well inside their own natural size: the 50-nucleotide strand has 295 Å of contour and a natural end-to-end of about 94 Å, while the attachment sites hold it at only 54 Å. A worm-like chain at less than its own rms size is under no tension at all, so the Marko–Siggia force is exactly zero and this construct is a genuine zero-force reference rather than a low-force one.

Why this matters for the interpretation

This is the construct that carries the argument in the next section. It is the same protein, the same two attachment sites, the same click chemistry, a comparable amount of DNA — and provably zero mechanical load. If the compression of the attachment sites were a force effect, this construct should show none of it. It shows 0.32 Å, which is as much as any duplex.

An earlier draft of this work described a 27-nucleotide strand as “taut” by comparing a 6.9 nm figure against a 6–7 nm span. That was an error: 6.9 nm is the rms end-to-end distance of a 27-mer, not its contour, and the contour is 15.9 nm. A chain is taut when the span approaches its contour, not its rms size, so the conclusion did not follow from the number. The 50-nucleotide strands used here are slack by either measure.

Is it acting as a spring at all?

eleven constructs, two proteins, two chemistries

The premise of the whole design is that the DNA acts as a spring: bend it, and it pushes the attachment sites apart in proportion to the force it delivers. That is a testable claim, and with eleven constructs measured against their own matched controls it can be tested rather than assumed.

Every construct that carries DNA compresses the sites. Ten of the eleven are negative, spanning −0.09 to −0.59 Å, and the eleventh is +0.02 — which is zero. Not one extends them, which is what a spring pushing its anchors apart would do.

And the size of the effect has nothing to do with the force:

  • Against the modelled spring force: r = +0.08, p = 0.81 — and the sign is positive, meaning more force goes with less compression.
  • Against how much of the protein the DNA touches: r = +0.32, p = 0.34.
  • Constructs with no spring at all — a slack single strand, or two separate arms that cannot circularise — compress by 0.28 Å. Those with a spring compress by 0.35 Å. The difference is not resolved (p = 0.54).
What this means

Attaching DNA to this protein moves the attachment sites together by about a third of an ångström, and it makes no measurable difference whether that DNA is a spring. A slack 50-nucleotide single strand under zero tension does it as well as a 27 bp duplex the model says is pushing with 6.6 pN.

This is the conclusion the companion ubiquitin study reached from NMR13 — that local protein–DNA interaction, not spring action, dominates — reproduced here independently, in a different protein, with a different attachment chemistry, and read out from a different observable. That agreement across two systems is the strongest thing in this report.

Two obvious mechanisms are not it. It is not the force, which does not correlate. And it is not simple contact area either, which also does not correlate: the 40 bp closed loop touches the barrel in only 20 % of frames and compresses the most of any duplex. What is common to every construct is a large, highly charged object tethered a couple of nanometres away; which specific part of that does the work is not something these runs identify.

Does closing the covalent loop matter?

five matched pairs

The rebuild described above changed one thing about the molecule: whether a covalent path runs from one attachment site, out along its tether, through the DNA, and back to the other. Everything else — protein, chemistry, spring, length, tether — is held fixed, which makes these five pairs a clean test of topology on its own.

pairclosed − two-arm (Å)p direction
27 bp-0.4720.007closing the loop compresses more
40 bp-0.2770.018closing the loop compresses more
40 bp nicked-0.1680.311closing the loop compresses more
50 nt ssDNA, sfGFP-0.0260.724closing the loop compresses more
50 nt ssDNA, ubiquitin+0.3240.126closing the loop compresses less

The three duplex pairs — the comparison the rebuild was designed to make — all point the same way: closing the loop compresses the sites further, by 0.31 Å on average, and two of the three clear significance on their own. Taken as a paired test across the three, p = 0.08 — suggestive, and not resolved at n = 3 pairs.

The two single-stranded pairs do not reproduce it. They give -0.026 Å and +0.324 Å — one is zero and the other has the opposite sign. Across all five pairs together the effect is p = 0.41: nothing.

Reading this honestly

There is a hint that covalent closure matters for a duplex and no evidence that it matters for a slack single strand — which would be physically sensible, since only a closed loop can transmit a bending moment around the circuit, and a slack strand has no moment to transmit. But a three-pair trend at p = 0.08 that reverses when two more pairs are added is a hypothesis, not a finding, and it is reported as one. The number of replicates that would settle it — six per system rather than three — is a day of GPU time whenever the allocation allows.

What the rebuild did establish is not statistical: the original build was not the molecule the experiment makes, and no amount of sampling would have fixed that. Correctness of the construct and significance of its effect are separate questions, and only the first one is settled here.

What the modification itself does

before any force is applied

Installing the two Tet2-Et residues shortens the Cβ–Cβ separation by 0.62 Å before any DNA is attached, and clicking gives most of it back. That is larger than any force effect in this study, so it is worth knowing what it is — and it is not a change in secondary structure. DSSP over residues 128–155 is identical in the wild type, the unclicked protein and the clicked adduct: site 133 is coil in every case and site 149 is 100% β in every case.

Site 133 is the clean result. Asp133 natively occupies the left-handed α region — positive φ — a conformation that Asp, Asn and Gly commonly adopt and that a phenylalanine-shaped side chain tolerates poorly. Tet2-Et is a phenylalanine derivative, and it is pushed 17.5° out in φ and 14° in ψ; clicking returns it to within a few degrees of wild type. The replicate spread is 0.5–0.8°, so this is not noise.

Site 149's ring stacks on Tyr200, but not reproducibly. The unclicked tetrazine averages ~10 heavy-atom contacts per frame, but the three replicates give 20.0, 10.4 and 0.9 — it samples stacked and unstacked states and three replicates cannot pin the occupancy. The clicked control is tight and low (0.68 ± 0.4 over nine replicates), yet the 40 bp chimeras stack again. So the ring at 149 can stack, and whether it does depends on the construct.

Both variables track the contraction. Across all 30–33 replicates carrying these residues, Cβ–Cβ correlates with the Tyr200 contact count (r = −0.68, p = 5×10⁻⁵, −38 mÅ per contact) and with φ at site 133 (r = −0.59, p = 3×10⁻⁴, −39 mÅ per degree); together they account for 55% of its variance. These are correlations across constructs that differ chemically, so this is suggestive rather than causal — but the contraction is local structure at the modified sites, and nothing to do with the spring.

Which positions can take Tet2-Et

Avoid positive-φ positions: the left-handed α region is occupied by Asp, Asn and Gly for a reason. Treat an aromatic neighbour as a liability, because the ring will stack on it in some constructs and not others, and because that stacking differs between the unclicked and clicked states — so it will masquerade as a mechanical effect for anyone using the unclicked protein as a reference. That is exactly how the retracted claim above arose. Ordinary β and α positions with no aromatic neighbour should be fine.

Which positions tolerate the modification

a design rule, tested in a second protein

The Ramachandran result above gives a rule with a prediction attached: a site strains on modification only where the native backbone occupies a positive-φ conformation, which Asp, Asn and Gly adopt readily and a bulkier side chain does not. Two proteins with two unrelated attachment chemistries give four sites to test it on, and exactly one of the four is positive-φ.

proteinsiteresiduenative φ, ψΔφ on modificationΔψnative conformation
sfGFP133ASP → TET+56.9, +16.3+17.5-13.9left-handed α
sfGFP149ASN → TET-126.6, +137.2+1.0-13.1ordinary
ubiquitin9CYS → CMS-81.4, +5.4-0.3-4.5ordinary
ubiquitin63CYS → CMS-56.1, +142.1+0.0+2.3ordinary

The prediction holds. The one positive-φ site moves 17.5° in φ; the three ordinary sites move by a degree or less. And the chemistries have nothing in common — sfGFP carries a genetically encoded tetrazine amino acid, a phenylalanine derivative installed by amber suppression; ubiquitin carries a cysteine converted to a maleimide thioether. What predicts the strain is not the adduct but the backbone conformation the native residue was holding.

The practical rule

When choosing attachment sites for either chemistry: avoid positions whose native φ is positive — in practice Gly, and the Asn/Asp positions that sit in the left-handed α region. An ordinary β or α position takes the modification without measurable backbone cost.

Treat an aromatic neighbour as a second liability, independently. The tetrazine ring at sfGFP’s site 149 stacks on Tyr200 in some constructs and not others, and it does so differently before and after clicking — so it will masquerade as a mechanical effect in exactly the comparison this project set out to make.

Both of these are conclusions about four sites in two proteins, which is a rule of thumb rather than a survey. What makes it worth stating is that the prediction was made from sfGFP alone and then held in a protein and a chemistry it was not derived from.

The network is intact everywhere, and the spring does not break it

Thr203 to the phenolate and Arg96 to the imidazolinone carbonyl2 hold at 96–100% in every system — these are the buried, load-bearing contacts that keep the chromophore planar, and nothing the spring does disturbs them. Gln94 holds at 91–97%. If the spring were prising the barrel open near the chromophore, these are the numbers that would fall, and they do not.

His148 is tighter in every chimera — but not beyond its own scatter

His148’s bond to the phenolate reads 72% in WT and 76% in the unclicked protein, against 80–81% in all three chimeras. The direction is consistent and mechanistically appealing — His148 sits between the two attachment sites, so a spring pulling on that strand plausibly presses it onto the chromophore. But the replicate-to-replicate spread is 58–92%, wider than the gap between the means. It is a hypothesis worth more sampling, not a result.

One apparent effect is an artefact of bistability

The His148 ND1-H -> chromophore phenolate contact — part of the proton relay behind the chromophore3 — reads about 30% in most systems and 0% in the 40 bp chimera, which looks like an effect and is not. Within a single system it is either near 0% or near 90%: a two-state Ser205 hydroxyl rotamer, flipped once per trajectory and then stuck. A mean of three coin flips is not a measurement, and figure 3 plots the individual replicates so it cannot pass as one. The automated check that flagged it lives in analysis/findings.py and runs over every H-bond.

Bridge planarity and cavity water are unchanged

systemτ twist (°)φ twist (°) waters within 6 Åmean RMSF (Å)

The two dihedrals that twist the chromophore out of plane — τ across the phenol–bridge bond and φ across the bridge–imidazolinone bond — are the structural proxy for non-radiative decay: the free chromophore, able to rotate about them, is essentially dark while the protein-bound one is bright4, so the wider their excursions the more of the excited state leaks away without a photon. They sit at 5–6° of twist in every system, with differences between systems of a few tenths of a degree against replicate spreads of similar size. Cavity water, the other route to quenching, is 8–11 molecules with spreads of 1–3. Neither is resolved. If the spring changes sfGFP’s brightness at these forces, 45 ns × 3 does not see the structural cause, and the honest reading of the fluorometry is that it needs either a stronger spring or far more sampling.

every panel ships the CSV it was drawn from

Force field and protocol

what every number above was computed with

Protein ff14SB14, DNA OL1515, TIP3P water18, Joung–Cheatham monovalent ions19 at 150 mM NaCl, and Mg²⁺ from the Li–Merz 12-6 set20 at ~5 mM for the duplex systems — 12-6 rather than 12-6-4 because OpenMM has no C⁴ term, so a 12-6-4 topology would silently lose the polarisation correction on import. Buffer and salt follow the companion ubiquitin experiment in this lab13.

The chromophore uses the published CRO parameters5, which come out of tleap24 at exactly −1.0000 e. The four custom residues — the tetrazine amino acid, the click adduct, and the DNA-side arm in its two forms — are typed with GAFF216 and charged with AM1-BCC17; their six backbone atoms are then overwritten with ff14SB’s types and charges so the peptide bonds into and out of the modified sites match every other one, the same device the chromophore parameters used5. Duplexes are built as ideal B-form DNA with PyMOL’s fnab28; the tethers are placed by superposition27 and torsion optimisation.

Simulations run in OpenMM 8.621 with the LangevinMiddle integrator22 at 300 K and a 4 fs timestep enabled by hydrogen-mass repartitioning on the solute only23, PME with a 0.9 nm cutoff, and a Monte Carlo barostat at 1 bar. Analysis uses MDTraj25; solvent accessibility is computed with Shrake–Rupley26.

How it is built

raw deposition → six systems
  1. 1

    Prepare build/01_protein

    2B3P → tleap-ready structure. Strips the crystallisation Cd²⁺ and acetate, keeps the buried cavity waters, assigns every histidine tautomer from its own H-bond geometry, and measures the attachment geometry everything downstream reads.

  2. 2

    Parameterise build/02_params

    Explicit atom and bond tables → RDKit → antechamber (AM1-BCC, GAFF2) → prepgen → backbone harmonisation → parmchk2. Zero parameters flagged for review across all four custom residues.

  3. 3

    Build the spring build/03_dna

    Ideal B-form duplex from PyMOL fnab, bent to the required span by mapping the helical axis onto a circular arc with each base pair moved as a rigid slab, so intra-pair geometry is preserved exactly and only the inter-pair geometry changes.

  4. 4

    Assemble build/04_assemble

    Tethers posed by backbone superposition plus torsion optimisation; the duplex docked onto the two target phosphate positions with its arc pushed away from the barrel; tleap driven in two passes so the ion count matches the water it dissolves in.

  5. 5

    Run runs, slurm

    Minimise → restrained NVT → staged NPT release → production at 4 fs with hydrogen-mass repartitioning on the solute only. Restart-safe, so preemption costs one checkpoint interval.

  6. 6

    Measure analysis

    Chromophore geometry and its H-bond network, protein and spring extension, where the duplex gives, barrel deformation, cavity water — then reduced to one row per replicate and one findings file the report renders.

Deliberately not used

The F ≈ 10 pN figure from Choi & Zocchi (2007)12. That paper labels it an upper bound from a worm-like-chain treatment that ignores kinking; the kinked model supersedes it and gives 1.5–2.4 pN for the same constructs. Using it would over-stress the protein roughly fourfold.

What this does and does not show

Does: that the chimera can be built and parameterised without inventing a force-field term; that the spring delivers 2–5 pN and 7–9 kBT by the model’s own formula evaluated on the simulation’s geometry; that a nick softens it in the predicted direction; that the barrel and the chromophore’s load-bearing hydrogen bonds survive intact; and that the protein is at least as stiff as Zocchi’s calibration assumes.

Does not: resolve the protein’s compliance, establish that the spring changes the chromophore, or confirm the kink the force model presumes. Those need the clicked control now running, more replicates, and longer trajectories — bash slurm/submit_all.sh --tier B extends every run to 300 ns from its checkpoint.
